3.text: this feat backwards. Then a huge kettle filled with boiling water is placed

4.text: by the side of a larch-tree. A thin pole with a sharp end protrudes from

5.text: the water. The competitors have to catch the end of a rope which hangs

6.text: from the larch-tree. Then they must jump into the kettle, alighting on the

7.text: end of the pole, and finally land safely on the ground. Other trials follow.

10.text: The “directions” of the evening are classed together as “Darkness”

11.text: (Wuˊs˙quus˙). They are not given separate sacrifices, except in special cases.

12.text: After the usual sacrifice to the Dawn, the Chukchee man will often sprinkle

13.text: a few drops of blood in the four principal “directions.” The darkness and

14.text: the midnight “directions” are frequently confused with the nadir (notaˊs˙qa-vaˊ-

15.text: ɪrg̣ɪn). Notaˊs˙qa-vaˊɪrg̣ɪn signifies literally “earth-being,” and the sacrifice in

16.text: that “direction” is sometimes meant as a sacrifice to the earth.²

17.text: Sun and Moon. — The Sun is generally described as a separate

18.text: vaˊɪrg̣ɪn. He is represented as a man in bright garments wandering around

19.text: the sky, drawn by dogs or reindeer. His reindeer are sometimes described

20.text: as having antlers of copper. He descended to earth along one of his own

21.text: rays, and married a girl, whom he carried with him to heaven by the same

22.text: road.³ He also brought to men a herd of white reindeer. The brown and

23.text: the gray reindeer come from under the ground, somewhere beyond the limits

24.text: of the peltry-bearing country (äviˊrɪ-nuˊtenut), at the place where the sky

25.text: touches the earth. There a large hole is bored through the ground, and

26.text: through that hole herds of reindeer pass continually, followed by wolves. In

27.text: this way the number of reindeer on earth increases.

28.text: The Sun goes down every evening to his wife, whose name is Walking-

29.text: around-Woman (Kavraˊ-ñña). According to another somewhat disconnected

30.text: version, Sun’s wife is called Rejoicing-Woman (Koˊrg̣ɪ-ña). This name was

31.text: given to her because she bore a son to her husband, and then said to him,

32.text: “Rejoice, I have a son!” The son was soon stolen by Stuck-Staff-Woman

33.text: (Uˊnpɪñe), who may sometimes be heard weeping in the open on very dark

34.text: nights at the end of summer. The Sun-People sought for the lost boy, but

35.text: the thief destroyed all traces of herself by sticking her magic staff across her

36.text: trail. This is how she received the name of Stuck-Staff-Woman. This episode

37.text: seems to be a fragment of some old tale.

38.text: The Moon is also considered a man, and to a certain extent holds a

39.text: position in contrast to that of the Sun. He is called the Sun of the keˊlᴇ.

40.text: The suns of lower worlds are often quite similar to our moon. Shamans
